name: PT Austindo Nusantara Jaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Austindo Nusantara Jaya: a First Resources estate at a price the float cannot arbitrage
frontmatter.summary: ANJT is a 40,136 ha pure palm estate controlled 91.2% by First Resources, with 94.6% of sales to related parties and a 1.6% free float. Through-cycle NAV is well above the share price, but the float and the group transfer-price mechanism mean the discount may not close; we initiate at BUY on fundamental value with an explicit liquidity warning.
thesis: Pure palm again: the West Papua estates were sold and the sago/edamame subsidiaries discontinued, so the FY2025 loss reflects a one-off divestment charge, not the operating business, whose operating profit was IDR878.5bn.

Through-cycle CPO value: our DCF on the house d.agri.cpo deck, calibrated to the FY2025 realised price, gives a fundamental value far above the price; the multiples cross-check disagrees and we say why.

The controlling shareholder is the business model: 94.6% of 9M 2026 revenue is sold to First Resources group companies on formula prices, and IDR1,124.0bn was lent to an affiliate in 2026 while IDR1,390.0bn was borrowed.
A 1.6% free float caps the re-rating: the engine applies a 20% liquidity discount and the stock still screens cheap, but position size, not conviction, is the binding constraint.
Dividends are the missing anchor: no payout for FY2023-FY2025, and the cash has gone to a group receivable rather than to shareholders.

catalysts.event: Monthly export levy/duty reset (combined charge cut a fifth to {{fact.F34}} in November) - if it holds, realised prices rise
FY2026 audited results - first clean year of First Resources ownership and the first test of the payout policy
AGM dividend decision on FY2026 profit

blocks.text: We initiate Austindo Nusantara Jaya (ANJT) at **BUY** with a target of **Rp2,919**, 120.4% above the Rp1,350 price. The target is built as 70% through-cycle DCF at Rp3,804 a share, 15% EV/EBITDA at Rp1,923 and 15% P/BV at Rp1,589, then cut by the engine's 20% liquidity discount for a 1.6% free float [S0, S3]. The discount alone takes the probability-weighted value from Rp3,649 to Rp2,919 a share; it is the largest single haircut in the bridge and the risks section shows why a float this thin earns it.

The company changed shape in 2025. First Resources became the controlling shareholder with 91.2%, the company converted to foreign-investment (PMA) status, the West Papua palm subsidiaries PT Permata Putera Mandiri and PT Putera Manunggal Perkasa were divested, and the sago and edamame businesses were discontinued [S3, S2]. What remains is a single-segment palm producer: 40,136 ha planted, 33,288 ha mature and 254 kt of CPO produced in FY2025 [S3, F7, F19, F5].

The FY2025 reported loss is not an operating loss. Revenue was IDR3,959.0bn and operating profit was IDR878.5bn, but a divestment loss of -72.1 USD m and a further loss from discontinued operations turned the year negative [S3, F20]. The 9M 2026 accounts show the cleaned-up business: revenue of IDR3,980.1bn, operating profit of IDR1,059.0bn and net profit of IDR811.2bn [S4].

The variant view is not about the CPO price, which the house deck already sets. It is about whether a minority holder can ever capture the value. 94.6% of 9M 2026 revenue was sold to First Resources group companies - PT Adhitya Serayakorita, PT Swadaya Mukti Prakarsa and PT Ciliandra Perkasa - under formula pricing [S4, F16]. In the same period the company borrowed IDR1,390.0bn long term and lent IDR1,124.0bn to PT Adhitya Serayakorita at eight and a half per cent [S4, F17, F23]. The asset is real; the question is who sets the price at which it is monetised.

Indonesian palm companies are usually valued on a through-cycle CPO price and an enterprise value per planted hectare, because a mature estate is a long-lived annuity whose earnings swing with a single commodity. When a strategic owner holds almost all the shares, the market price often sits below fundamental value for years because there is no free float to arbitrage the gap; that is a feature of the ownership structure, not a temporary mispricing.

ANJT is an upstream palm producer. It grows fresh fruit bunches (FFB) on its own estates, buys FFB from third-party suppliers and plasma cooperatives, and mills it into crude palm oil (CPO) and palm kernel. In FY2025 own FFB production was 768 kt and third-party purchases were 472 kt, so close to two-fifths of the 1,234 kt milled was bought-in fruit [S3]. CPO production was 254 kt at an oil extraction rate of 20.6%, and palm kernel production was 51.6 kt [S3, F5, F26, F27].

The footprint after the divestments sits in four Indonesian provinces: Belitung, where 17,360 ha is operated by PT Sahabat Mewah dan Makmur; West Kalimantan at Ketapang; North Sumatra at Siais, where 9,412 ha is operated by PT Austindo Nusantara Jaya Agri Siais; and South Sumatra [S3, F36, F37]. Planted area is 40,136 ha of which 33,288 ha is mature, so roughly five-sixths of the estate is already producing. The remainder is 6,848 ha of immature estate; at the company's own FFB yield and oil extraction rate it adds a further slice of CPO a year once mature, which is why the volume curve in the financial section rises from FY2028E instead of staying flat [S3, F7, F19, F26, F49]. The plasma schemes sit alongside it, and both are the growth option rather than a funded capex programme [S3].

The milling intake is the commercial core. Because close to two-fifths of the fruit is bought in, ANJT's margin depends on the CPO-to-FFB spread, not only on its own yield; when CPO rises, bought-in FFB costs rise with it, which is why the FY2026 cost base moved up [S3, S4]. In 2026 the company also began buying finished palm products for resale - IDR717.9bn in nine months - which lifted reported revenue and cost of revenue without changing the estate or its production capacity [S4, F24]. That trading book is small relative to the estate asset but large relative to reported profit, and it is the main reason reported revenue growth overstates operating growth in FY2026E [S4].

Strategy under First Resources is consolidation rather than expansion. The company replanted 1,472 ha in 2025, mainly at ANJA and SMM, and obtained RSPO certification for all nucleus, plasma and partnership plantations in early 2025 [S3, F28]. No new estate or mill was announced. ANJ Boga, ANJ Agri Papua and Gading Mas Indonesia Teguh were discontinued with effect from the end of 2025, with no material adverse impact stated [S2]. The disposal of the West Papua subsidiaries and the discontinuation of the sago and edamame businesses leave a single-segment palm producer whose reported numbers are comparable with its plantation peers for the first time [S3, S2].

ANJT is a challenger, not a leader. At 254 kt of CPO a year it is a mid-cap planter, far behind the largest Indonesian groups, and its scale advantage is the mill intake rather than the land bank [S3]. The controlling shareholder is First Resources Limited with 91.2%; the public free float is 1.6%, and the company has been a PMA entity since the change of control [S0, S3]. Management's stated rationale for the acquisition was to secure feedstock for First Resources' downstream operations, which frames the estate as a supplier inside a group value chain rather than an independent marketer of its own crop [S3]. That is the strategic logic and also the source of the minority's discount.

Indonesian palm is a volume-and-price industry with almost no product differentiation: the oil is a commodity, the buyer sets the reference, and the producer's only durable lever is cost per tonne and the quality of the estate [S3, S6]. ANJT's economics are therefore set by three external variables - the CPO price, the export levy and duty wedge, and the rupiah - plus one internal variable, the share of mill intake bought from third parties rather than grown on its own land [S3, S4].

The house deck carries CPO at US$1,135/t for FY2026E, US$1,240/t for FY2027E and US$1,180/t by FY2029E against a FY2025 actual of US$1,007/t [deck: d.agri.cpo]. ANJT realised US$871/t a tonne in FY2025 and US$822/t in FY2024, below the benchmark in both years because the export charge and the group sales formula sit between the estate and the world price [S3, F3, F4]. The realisation ratio in the model is calibrated on the last actual, not on a forecast spike, so the engine carries the structural discount rather than a favourable year into the long run [S3, S4].

The deck is not a spot forecast, and the gap matters. The November 2026 government reference price is US$979/t [S6], about a seventh below the FY2026E deck of US$1,135/t and a fifth below the FY2027E deck; the house deck is the through-cycle series and the base case applies the FY2025-calibrated realisation of 86.5% to it rather than to the monthly reference price [deck: d.agri.cpo] [S3]. The gap is deliberate: the HPE is a monthly administrative reference set off recent spot, while the house deck is the through-cycle path the method card requires, and the FY2027E premium reflects the El Nino supply loss rather than a spot call [S5, S6]. The bear case and the lower rows of the sensitivity table test exactly that gap - a benchmark near today's reference price with realisation held at 86.5% - so the risk that the deck is too high is in the numbers, not just in the prose [S6].

The wedge is the export charge. In November 2026 the combined levy and duty fell a fifth to US$246/t a tonne, a much sharper cut than the fall in the reference price, and the schedule is reset monthly off that reference [S6]. If the lower charge held, the realisation ratio would move toward nine-tenths; we do not carry it in the base case, because the schedule is administrative and reverses as readily as it falls, but it is modelled as a realisation shock in the bull case so the value of a sustained cut is visible [S6]. This is the single most volatile line between the deck price and the price the company actually books, and it is the reason a headline CPO move does not translate one-for-one into earnings.

Supply is the swing factor. The trade press reports that El Nino is expected to cut Indonesian palm output by about 2.2 Mt in 2027 versus 2026, which supports prices into next year and caps ANJT's own volume [S5]. We take a small volume haircut in FY2027E and no more, because ANJT's estates are in Sumatra, Belitung and Kalimantan rather than the worst-hit areas and because the decline is a national estimate rather than company guidance [S3, S5]. The same weather that supports the price therefore compresses the volume, so the net earnings effect is smaller than either headline.

Competitive position. Judged on the estate, the cost base is stable rather than squeezed, and that is as far as the evidence goes. Total palm production cost was IDR2,090.8bn in 9M 2026 [S4]; less D&A of IDR200.9bn that is about Rp8.22m/t [F40], flat to down on 9M 2025, when total production cost was IDR2,157.3bn and mature-plantation maintenance was IDR311.9bn [S4, F50, F51]. We do not rank that number against other planters: the filing carries no peer series and no cost curve is archived, so the ranking would be an assertion rather than a sourced fact, and the observed cost per tonne is the only benchmark we can defend [S4]. The US$646.6 per tonne that the model carries is the blended cost of the tonne it sells: it also carries IDR717.9bn of finished goods bought for resale at a near-zero spread [S4, F24]. The high-cost label that the blended number would attract belongs to that pass-through book, not to the estate. What remains is price risk rather than trough-mortality risk, because the estate keeps producing at a low margin in a trough rather than ceasing to produce - which is why the bear case is an earnings event driven by CPO and the export charge, and why the through-cycle DCF rather than a spot-earnings multiple is the right primary method [S4, S6].

Five forces. Supplier power is moderate and rising, because close to two-fifths of mill intake is bought from third parties whose FFB price is set off the same CPO reference [S3]. Buyer power is extreme by construction: one group buys 94.6% of revenue [S4, F16]. Barriers to entry are high - land, permits, RSPO certification and mills - protecting the incumbent estates but not the minority's economics [S3]. Substitution is slow, with palm competing against soya and sunflower oil in the same vegetable-oil complex [deck: d.agri.soyoil]. Rivalry is on cost, not brand, and the group's downstream demand gives ANJT a captive buyer that a standalone planter does not have [S3, S4].

Palm oil is the world's most consumed vegetable oil because it is the cheapest per tonne of any oilseed crop. Indonesia and Malaysia supply most of the world's exports, and Indonesian policy has for a decade used export levies to fund a domestic biodiesel mandate, which links the domestic price to the export price through a formula rather than a free market.

Revenue and volume. FY2025 revenue was IDR3,959.0bn on 270 kt of CPO-equivalent sales [S3, F1]. The PK leg is converted at each year's own realised PK/CPO price ratio, taken from the realised CPO and PK prices on the same page [F43, F44], so FY2025's 270 kt against FY2024's 275 kt is a fall of about one and a half per cent, not the larger fall a single fixed ratio would imply. For FY2026E we model 300.0 kt, set from the 9M 2026 actual rather than a company plan: revenue of IDR3,980.1bn is a third above the same period a year earlier, which after a price and rupiah effect implies a volume increase in the low double digits and includes the new resale book [S4, F12, F24]. FY2027E drops to 293.0 kt on the El Nino [S3, S5]. From FY2028E the volume follows the maturity of the 6,848 ha of immature estate rather than a flat cap: 300.0 kt, 310.0 kt and 325.0 kt by FY2030E, and 330.0 kt in the long run, which is the estate's own capacity at its own yield and extraction rate [F7, F19, F26, F49]. The FY2026E revenue line is not a clean like-for-like: it carries a trading book that earns a thin margin on top of the estate's own production [S4].

Margins and costs. The most important line is cash cost per tonne, and it has two components that must not be confused. The estate: total palm production cost of IDR2,090.8bn in 9M 2026 [S4] less IDR200.9bn of D&A is about Rp8.22m/t [F40], against the same figure in FY2025 calculated the same way from cost of revenue of IDR2,562.0bn less restated D&A of IDR304.6bn [S3, F10]. The estate cost is therefore flat to down: a stable cost base, not a squeezed one, which is what the filing lets us say without a peer cost curve [S4]. The pass-through: IDR717.9bn of finished goods bought for resale in the nine months [S4, F24], sold at a near-zero spread, which lifts both revenue and cost of revenue without touching the estate. Adding the two gives the nine-month cash cost of IDR2,804.9bn less IDR200.9bn and the model's blended US$646.6 per tonne [S4, F13, F14]. The model carries the blended number because the tonne and the revenue it books are blended; the estate-only cost, which is what competes with other planters, is the Rp8.22m/t figure. We hold the FY2026 level in real terms and escalate it with inflation, with no unexplained margin squeeze in the base case [S4].

Earnings quality. Accruals are not the constraint. Operating cash flow of IDR947.8bn in 9M 2026 covered net profit of IDR811.2bn, so the reported profit is cash-backed and the Sloan-style test does not flag the name [S4, F22, F29]. The composition of revenue is the flag: 94.6% of revenue is related-party, and a IDR1,124.0bn receivable from PT Adhitya Serayakorita sits in non-current assets at eight and a half per cent [S4, F16, F17]. That receivable is a large share of market capitalisation; we carry it at face value in the bridge and treat its recovery as a governance risk rather than a base-case haircut, because nothing in the filing suggests impairment and a unilateral haircut would be a forecast dressed as conservatism [S4].

Balance sheet. At the end of September 2026 cash was IDR1,149.1bn against short-term bank debt of IDR992.3bn and long-term bank debt of IDR1,268.4bn, so gross bank debt is roughly twice cash and net debt is IDR1,181.0bn, up from the IDR723.0bn reported at the start of the year because the long-term facility funded the group loan [S4, F30, F31, F32, F48]. Equity is IDR4,610.8bn and minority interests are a small deficit, so the parent's claim is essentially the whole book [S4, F33]. The company is not in net cash: it carries net debt equal to well under one year of FY2026E EBITDA [S4]. Two cautions on the model here. The engine's pro-forma forecast balance sheet rolls forward from the December 2025 pack accounts and does not seed the September 2026 actuals, so its forecast cash and net-debt path is not usable; the valuation uses the September 2026 bridge of IDR1,181.0bn instead [S4]. And the interest line is carried at the 8.8% mid-point of the facility band the LK discloses, charged on the opening debt stock: that makes FY2026E interest of IDR85.8bn understate the year after the 2026 drawdown, while the IDR205.1bn carried from FY2027E is what the September debt stock implies at that rate [S4]. The rate itself is not flattered - the cash interest actually paid in the nine months averages well below it [S4].

Capex and working capital. 9M 2026 capex was IDR204.1bn, covering replanting and mill upkeep rather than expansion, and FY2025 capex was IDR248.4bn [S3, F15]. We hold capex near the recent run-rate, because a mature estate of this size needs replanting capex but no new land, and the replanting programme is the main discretionary call [S3, S4]. Working capital is held at 16% of revenue; the higher observed ratio is inflated by the group receivable, which is a financing item rather than a trading balance [S4, S0].

Capital allocation. No dividend was paid for FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025; the last cash dividend relates to FY2022 [S3, S0]. In 2026 the generated cash went to a IDR1,124.0bn loan to a related party instead, funded by IDR1,390.0bn of new long-term bank debt [S4, F17, F23]. We model a 20% payout from FY2026 because a controlling owner of 91.2% normally wants cash out, but the 2026 decision points the other way and the dividend is not an anchor in this name [S3, S4]. The tax rate we carry is 22%, in line with the effective charge in the filings [S4]. Terminal growth is 2.5% nominal, set from the deck's own post-FY2029 price path rather than the top of the house range. The estate is planted out and capex roughly equals D&A because replanting maintains rather than expands the asset, but the deck settles CPO at US$1,150/t long run against US$1,180/t in FY2029 while the cash cost keeps escalating with rupiah inflation, so real FCFF does not grow [S3, deck: d.agri.cpo]. Carrying the top of the house range would assume real growth the price path does not deliver and charge no reinvestment against it; at 2.5% the DCF is consistent with the deck, and the sensitivity table's benchmark axis shows that the price path, not the terminal rate, is what moves the value [deck: d.agri.cpo].

Why this method set. A palm estate is a long-lived, single-commodity cash-flow stream, so a through-cycle DCF is primary; the multiples are cross-checks, because FY2026E is a mid-cycle year and capitalising mid-cycle EBITDA is the procyclical error the house method forbids [S4, deck: d.agri.cpo]. We weight DCF 70%, EV/EBITDA 15% and P/BV 15%. The DCF owns the valuation because it is the only method that prices the deck path, the mature/immature mix and the terminal estate value in one consistent framework [S3].

The cost of capital is 11.3%: a 7.4% rupiah risk-free rate, a 4.2% mature-market equity risk premium, a 2.5% country risk premium, an unlevered beta of 0.80 levered to 1.12 at 0.51 debt/equity, a 13.3% cost of equity and a 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt [S0].

The rupiah rate is the right discount rate because costs are rupiah-denominated and revenue is dollar-linked; the country premium captures the policy risk in the export-charge schedule, and we do not add a second, ad hoc governance premium on top of the liquidity discount [S0, S6]. The cost of debt needs a word because two rates appear in the packet. The engine discounts at its kd_pre_tax of 9.4%, which is the macro-deck rupiah risk-free rate plus the corporate credit spread [deck: macro]. The interest line uses 8.8%, and that rate is derived, not disclosed: the rupiah term facilities price at compounded three-month IndONIA plus three and a quarter per cent, with a six and a quarter per cent floor, and the BRI overdraft at five and a quarter per cent [S4, p.50], so there is no fixed coupon to read off the filing. We anchor on what the company actually paid: cash interest of IDR106.3bn in 9M 2026 [F55], annualised, against bank debt that roughly doubled between the December 2025 and September 2026 balance sheets (IDR992.3bn short-term plus IDR1,268.4bn long-term at the September date) [S4, F31, F32], which puts the effective rate at the figure the model carries, broadly consistent with the formula at the macro-deck BI rate of 5.75 [deck: macro]. The floor is therefore not binding. That rate sits under a percentage point below the WACC kd of 9.4% because the WACC prices marginal market debt while the P&L prices facilities whose spread was fixed at drawdown, and we keep them separate on purpose: collapsing the two would either flatter the discount rate or overstate interest. It is not a value-relevant gap, because debt peaks on the September 2026 balance sheet and the group turns to net cash in FY2027E [S4, F31, F32]. The WACC itself cannot be flexed independently in the engine because it is built from the macro deck, so the sensitivity is disclosed rather than tabulated: the equity weight is 66.0% and the debt weight 34.0%, so a lower cost of debt used in both places would lower the WACC toward the cost of equity and raise the DCF [S0, S4, deck: macro].

At the deck price, with an average volume of 300.0 kt across the forecast, the calibrated realisation and costs escalating with inflation, the DCF gives Rp3,804 a share, of which 52.8% is terminal value [deck: d.agri.cpo]. Two things support it: the estate is five-sixths mature and needs no growth capex, and the deck is the house through-cycle series rather than spot, which sits below the FY2027E deck price [S3, deck: d.agri.cpo]. A high terminal share is normal for a plantation with a finite but long-lived asset base, and the sensitivity table shows how much of the value sits in the last few years [S3].

The estate also prices sensibly per hectare, the way Indonesian planters are traded. The DCF enterprise value of IDR12,823.8bn over 40,136 ha planted hectares is 319.4 million rupiah per planted hectare, and 385.1 million per mature hectare on 33,288 ha [S3, F7, F19, F45, F46]. At Rp1,350 the market's enterprise value - IDR4,528.1bn of equity plus IDR1,181.0bn of September net debt - is 142.2 million per planted hectare and 171.5 million per mature hectare [S0, S4, F47, F52]. The DCF is therefore roughly twice the market's per-hectare value; the gap is the immature 6,848 ha and the deck price that the market is not paying for, and a 1.6% float gives it no reason to [S3, S0]. The grid is the cross-check the method card asks for: the observed estate cash cost of Rp8.22m/t is the only cost benchmark the filing supports [S4, F40], so the per-hectare gap cannot be written off as a high-cost estate that deserves a discount - but nor is it evidence of a cost advantage, because no peer cost curve is archived to rank it against. The leverage check sits alongside it: net debt of IDR1,181.0bn is about one times the FY2025 actual EBITDA of IDR1,183.1bn, so interest is covered even at trough earnings and this is a valuation and governance story rather than a solvency one [S4, F48]. The dividend is real but small against the asset: a 20% payout gives a 4.2% yield at the current price against a DCF value of Rp3,804 [S0].

The cross-checks disagree, and the reason is measurable. The EV/EBITDA leg applies 7.4 times the data pack's LTM EBITDA, not FY2026E EBITDA: the pack's LTM figure is below even the restated FY2025A EBITDA of IDR1,183.1bn because its direct-method cash-flow statement books depreciation as a cash inflow, so the LTM EBITDA is understated and the leg comes out at Rp1,923, -49.5% against the DCF [S0, S3]. On our restated FY2026E EBITDA of IDR1,559.9bn the same multiple would capitalise a far larger number, so we treat the printed leg as a conservative floor rather than a fair-value cross-check rather than describing it as an FY2026E multiple [S0]. P/BV at 1.2 times gives Rp1,589, -58.2% against it, on a book value that carries the estate at historical cost [S0, S4]. Both divergences are therefore data-pack and accounting artefacts, not evidence that the DCF is wrong. At Rp1,350 the equity is IDR4,528.1bn against September net debt of IDR1,181.0bn, so the market capitalises FY2026E EBITDA on the restated earnings at a low single-digit multiple once the actual debt is counted - and the DCF says that is too cheap [S0, S4]. The target uses the DCF but is cut by the 20% liquidity discount, because a value a minority cannot realise is not a value it can bank [S0].

What the price implies. At Rp1,350 the reverse DCF returns an implied CPO price of US$1,089 per tonne on the FY2027E deck - about 88% of the deck, close to the US$1,180/t spot and above the November reference price of US$979/t - not a value per share [S0, S6]. Read correctly, it says the market is pricing CPO a little below the house through-cycle deck and well above the monthly reference price, which is consistent with a float that cannot arbitrage the gap and with the governance discount for the related-party sales and the receivable [S0, S4, S6].

shows the bridge from enterprise value to equity, including the IDR1,124.0bn group receivable carried at face value. The bridge is where the minority's problem is visible: the operating value is real, but a large slice of the asset value is a claim on a group company rather than cash in the estate [S4].

Liquidity and float (high likelihood, high impact). The free float is 1.6% with three-month average daily value traded of IDR116.0m a day [S0]. That is tens of thousands of shares a day, so the float changes hands only over years of average turnover and a fund cannot build or exit a meaningful position [S0]. The 20% is not an assertion: it is the house liquidity schedule's band for a name at this turnover, and the schedule steps to a larger discount only below a materially lower daily value, so this stock sits at the conservative end of the 20% band rather than at the maximum [S0]. The cost is visible in the target: the discount takes Rp3,649 down to Rp2,919 a share, the largest single haircut in the bridge. That is the single reason a large upside is not actionable at size, and it is why the target is presented as a fundamental value with an explicit warning rather than as a trade recommendation [S0, S3].

Related-party pricing (high likelihood, medium impact). 94.6% of revenue is sold to First Resources group entities on formula prices [S4, F16]. The formula is disclosed as a variance adjustment against a reference, but a controlling owner sets both sides of the trade. A change in the formula would move realisation without any change in volume, and the effect would land directly in the DCF's revenue line [S4]. That is the cleanest way for value to leave the minority without a visible operational event [S3, S4].

Governance and structure (medium likelihood, high impact). IDR1,124.0bn was lent to PT Adhitya Serayakorita at eight and a half per cent while IDR1,390.0bn was borrowed long term to fund it [S4, F17, F23]. The receivable is a large share of market capitalisation and unsecured in substance; a write-down would remove a material part of our target [S4]. The mitigation is that the loan is interest-bearing and disclosed, so this is an optics-class structure flag rather than a manipulation-class one; the risk is economic, not forensic [S4].

Commodity (medium likelihood, high impact). A fall in CPO toward marginal cost would hit estate earnings hard through the price, not through the cost base: the estate cash cost of Rp8.22m/t is observed and stable [F40], so the estate survives a trough but its profit still falls to a low level, and that is the bear case [S4, deck: d.agri.cpo]. The estate does not stop producing in a trough; it produces at a low margin, which is why the bear valuation is a real number rather than a zero [S3].

Regulation (medium likelihood, medium impact). Levy and duty schedules reset monthly [S6]; the November cut is a tailwind, a reversal is not, and the biodiesel mandate that funds the levy is a policy choice rather than a market clearing price [S6].

FX (medium-to-high likelihood, medium impact). Costs are rupiah and revenue is dollar-linked, so a weaker rupiah helps, and the model does not assume a flat currency: the house macro deck runs the rupiah from 17,570 in FY2026E to 18,350 in FY2027E and 19,000 in the long run, which adds roughly a tenth to IDR revenue against a flat rate [deck: macro]. That is a driver, not a background assumption, and it is why the financial and valuation sections state the FX path rather than leaving it in the deck. The reversal is a live risk: spot JISDOR is 18,140 [S6], and the bear case appreciates the rupiah by a twentieth - the mirror of the bull's depreciation - which removes a slice of that lift [deck: macro] [S6].

Operational (low likelihood, medium impact). Fire and flood are the physical risks: hotspots were detected in 2025 and a few were verified inside planted areas, and El Nino is the 2027 yield risk [S3, S5]. RSPO certification mitigates market access risk in Europe but does not insure the crop [S3].

The scenarios are mirrored on four drivers, so neither case is a stack of one-sided haircuts: bear and bull move the CPO deck by a fifth, volume by a twentieth, realisation by about a twentieth (the export charge reversing versus the November cut holding; the bull carries the levy cut as a realisation shock, so its value is in the bull number rather than only in the prose [S6]) and the rupiah by a twentieth (appreciation versus depreciation), in opposite directions, at 25%, 50% and 25% probabilities [S0, S4]. Each case is valued at today's date and then rolled forward a year at the 13.3% cost of equity, net of that case's own next-twelve-month dividend rather than one common figure: Rp57 in the base case, nothing in the bear case because a trough year pays no dividend, and a larger amount in the bull case, where the payout is set by that case's earnings. That is what reproduces the printed twelve-month values: base Rp3,190 to Rp3,558, bear Rp527 to Rp597 and bull Rp6,194 to Rp6,881 [S0]. Weighting those at the probabilities gives Rp3,649, and the 20% discount takes the target to Rp2,919; that is the whole target construction, and
prints the same set [S0]. In the bear case the group receivable is also the asset most at risk, which is why we flag it rather than mirror it with a separate shock [S4].

Signposts that would change the view: a dividend declaration for FY2026; any change to the related-party sales formula; repayment or extension of the IDR1,124.0bn receivable; a free-float increase from a First Resources selldown - a cure to the IDX free-float minimum would remove the 20% discount outright and is the single largest value event available to the minority; and the audited FY2026 estate cost per tonne, which tells us whether the observed cost base is real rather than a quarterly artefact [S3, S4].

Ownership and control. First Resources Limited holds 91.2% after the 2025 takeover; insiders hold 95.9% and institutions 0.0% [S3, S0, F38]. The company converted to PMA status and replaced its board at an extraordinary meeting in May 2025 [S3]. With a 1.6% float, the minority has no vote that matters and no exit route at scale, so governance is not a theoretical overlay but the main determinant of the realised return [S3, S0].

Related parties. 9M 2026 revenue was sold overwhelmingly to related parties: Adhitya Serayakorita, Swadaya Mukti Prakarsa and Ciliandra Perkasa, all First Resources group companies [S4, F16]. The company also buys from related parties, with Limpah Sejahtera among its trade payables [S4]. This is the modal value-destruction channel on IDX and it is running at almost the whole of revenue; the relevant question is whether the formula is fair, not whether the sales are related [S3, S4].

Pledged shares and board. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the annual report [S3]. The board was reconstituted in 2025 with a new President Commissioner and a new President Director after the change of control, which is normal for a new owner but leaves the independent directors with little leverage [S3].

Auditor and opinion. The FY2025 statements carry an unmodified opinion. The auditor's emphasis of matter draws attention to the restatement note and describes the prior-period errors as the remeasurement of accounts in the functional currency and the impairment of fixed assets, and states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter [S3, p.264]. That is a disclosed correction, not a cash item - an optics-class flag - but it is a reminder that the accounting changed hands with the ownership [S3].

Dividend record. Nil for FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025; the policy has no fixed ratio and the AGM decides annually [S3, S0]. With earnings now positive and the group loan funded, the first real test of capital allocation comes with the FY2026 decision [S3, S4].

ESG. ANJT obtained RSPO certification for all nucleus, plasma and partnership plantations in early 2025, a commercial asset in European markets [S3]. Fire incidence was low, with a few verified spots inside planted areas in 2025, and the estate-level controls are disclosed [S3]. The methane-capture biogas electricity business is small but is a genuine emissions reduction and a low-cost sustainability signal to buyers [S3].
November 2026: the levy and duty reset, with the combined charge already cut a fifth to US$246/t; whether it holds into December is the first signpost [S6].

March 2027: FY2026 audited results - the first clean year under First Resources, and the test of whether the blended cost is only the resale pass-through while the estate cost stays at about 8.2 IDR m/t a tonne, and whether the 94.6% related-party sales ratio is the new normal [S3, S4].
June 2027: the AGM dividend decision on FY2026 profit, the first year with the earnings to pay one [S3].

KPIs we watch: monthly CPO and PK volumes (CPO production was 254 kt in FY2025), the realised CPO price against the deck, cost of revenue per tonne, the related-party receivable balance, and any change in the free float [S3, S4, F5].

We also track the monthly export-charge schedule, because a sustained lower charge would lift realisation without any change in the deck, and any First Resources announcement on the role the estate plays in its downstream supply chain [S6, S3].

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: CPO-equivalent tonnage sold
assumptions.basis: The volume key is CPO-equivalent tonnes, priced off one benchmark: FY2025 CPO sales of 229.333 kt plus PK at the realised 0.840 PK/CPO price ratio (USD 732 against USD 871 [F43]) give 270.07 kt [F1], against 274.80 kt in FY2024 at that year's realised 0.609 ratio (USD 501 against USD 822 [F44]) [F2]. FY2026E is set from the 9M-2026 actual rather than a plan: revenue of Rp3,980.1bn [F12] is 33.3% above 9M-2025 against a price and rupiah effect, and at the deck realisation that is ~300 kt for the year. FY2027E takes 2% off to 293 kt on the El Nino that the trade press reports cutting Indonesian output by ~2.2 Mt [S5], then the volume follows a maturity curve rather than a flat cap: 6,848 ha of the 40,136 ha planted are immature (40,136 less 33,288 mature [F7, F19]), which at the company's own 21.39 t/ha FFB yield [F8] and 20.60% OER [F26] is ~30 kt of CPO a year when it comes into production. We phase that in: 300 kt FY2028E, 310 kt FY2029E and 325 kt FY2030E, with 330 kt in the long run - the 2025 replanting of 1,471.84 ha [S3] and the immature area, not a new estate. The company guides nothing publicly, so this is the estate's own capacity curve, not a growth plan.

assumptions.label: Realised CPO price / d.agri.cpo benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual and held flat: FY2025 realised CPO of USD 871/t [F3] over the FY2025 benchmark of USD 1,007/t is 0.865, after 0.854 in FY2024 [F4] and 0.825 in FY2023, so the wedge is the export levy plus duty and the domestic/export mix, not a trend. No default haircut is applied to the deck, and no premium either: the realised price is what the company actually booked against the same benchmark. The November-2026 schedule cut the combined levy and duty 20% to USD 246.36/t [S6], which would lift the ratio toward 0.90, but the schedule is reset monthly off the reference price so it is not carried as permanent - it is a bull-case lever, not the base.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DMO reference-price mechanism applies to crude palm oil sold into the domestic biodiesel programme, and ANJT sells CPO and PK to commercial buyers including the First Resources group at formula prices [S4]; no share of volume is administratively capped.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (no overburden in a plantation)
assumptions.basis: Palm cost is expressed per tonne of product sold, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and the whole cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no strip-ratio analogue on an estate [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Total cash cost per CPO-equivalent tonne sold - estate plus resale pass-through - ex-D&A and ex-SG&A (IDR)
assumptions.basis: This is the BLENDED unit cost on the tonne the model sells, not the estate cost, and the split matters. Estate-only: total palm production cost 9M-2026 was Rp2,090.8bn [F39, F40]; less 9M D&A of Rp200.9bn [F14] that is Rp1,889.9bn, or about Rp8.22m/t on the 9M volume - flat to down from Rp8.31m/t in FY2025 (pack COGS Rp2,562bn less restated D&A Rp304.6bn [F10] over 270.07 kt [F1]), so the estate cost is stable to down. We do not rank it against other planters: the filing carries no peer or cost-curve series, so the observed Rp8.22m/t is the only benchmark we can source [S4]. On top sits the resale pass-through: Rp717.9bn of finished goods bought in 9M 2026 [F24], which enters cost of revenue [F13] and is sold at a near-zero spread. 1,889.9 + 717.9 = Rp2,611.6bn of 9M cash cost on ~230 kt = Rp11.36m/t blended, of which ~Rp3.14m/t is the pass-through. The model keeps the blended number because the tonne it sells and the revenue it books are blended; dropping the pass-through from cost without dropping its revenue would overstate EBITDA by the whole Rp717.9bn. We then escalate at 4% nominal, the rupiah inflation assumption in the macro deck, with no real margin squeeze either way. Bought-in FFB, 38% of mill intake [F9], is priced off CPO and is inside the estate cost.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cost
assumptions.basis: Not separately modelled: diesel and fertiliser move with the rupiah and the CPO-linked FFB price already inside cost_per_bcm, so a fuel split would double count [S4].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Milling, haulage and port cost are already inside the per-tonne cash cost backed out of the cost-of-revenue note [F13, F14]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: a plantation pays no production royalty and the FY2025 and 9M-2026 statements carry no royalty line; the export duty and levy are borne at shipment and are inside realisation [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (renewable energy, FFB, nursery)
assumptions.basis: Left at zero: the methane/biogas electricity sales and FFB sales are small and are already inside the revenue base that the 270-300 kt CPO-equivalent volume is calibrated to [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Not used because other_revenue is zero; kept at the engine default [S3].

assumptions.label: D&A per CPO-equivalent tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E: 9M depreciation of Rp200.9bn [F14] annualised to ~Rp262bn over 300 kt, about Rp0.87m/t; FY2025 was Rp304.6bn [F10] over 270.07 kt, Rp1.13m/t, but the divested West Papua assets and the lower fixed-asset base cut the charge ~14%. Thereafter it escalates at 4% with the asset base rather than falling to the data pack's Rp3.1bn, which is the direct-method cash-flow artifact, not the P&L charge.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per CPO-equivalent tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 additions were Rp204.1bn (PP&E Rp108.7bn plus bearer plants Rp95.4bn) [F15], about Rp266bn for the year on 300 kt, or Rp0.89m/t; FY2025 was Rp244.1bn on 270.07 kt, Rp0.90m/t, so the intensity is stable. It covers replanting (1,471.84 ha in 2025 [S3]) and mill upkeep; no expansion capex is assumed because the company has not announced a new estate or mill.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no mill or new estate is under construction after the West Papua divestment; the remaining growth capex is plasma development for the cooperatives, which is recovered through plasma receivables [S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default 16.3% (average of FY2023A-FY2025A). The 9M-2026 balance sheet shows working capital of Rp992.6bn on Rp3,980.1bn of revenue, 24.9%, inflated by a related-party receivable that is a financing item, not trade; we keep the historical operating ratio rather than a one-off [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22%, the Indonesian statutory corporate rate from 2026, against 18.8% actually paid in 9M-2026 (Rp188.4bn on Rp1,004.3bn pre-tax) and a 23.6% three-year average [S4, S0]; the 2026 rate benefits from final-taxed interest and non-taxable dividend income that will not repeat.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.8%, derived from the observed rate, not lifted from a disclosed band. The rupiah term facilities price at compounded 3M IndONIA plus 3.25% with a 6.25% floor, and the BRI overdraft at 5.25% [S4 p.50] - a formula, not a fixed coupon. What the company actually paid is the anchor: cash interest paid of Rp106.3bn in 9M-2026 [F55] annualises to about Rp141.7bn, against interest-bearing bank debt moving from Rp975.5bn at 31 December 2025 [S0] to Rp2,260.6bn at 30 September 2026 (short-term Rp992.3bn [F31] plus long-term Rp1,268.4bn [F32]). On the average balance of Rp1,618bn that is 8.8%; on the period-end balance it is 6.3%, but the period-end denominator flatters the rate because the Rp1,124bn related-party loan and the debt that funded it were drawn during the year. With the BI rate at 5.75% [deck: macro] a compounded 3M IndONIA near 5.4% plus the 3.25% spread gives about 8.7%, so the paid rate and the formula agree and the 6.25% floor is not binding. We carry 8.8% flat and apply it to every forecast year and to both the interest line and the debt stock. It sits 0.6pp below the engine's WACC kd_pre_tax of 9.4% because the WACC prices marginal market debt (macro-deck rf plus corporate spread) while the P&L prices facilities whose spread was fixed at drawdown; section 4 shows the two side by side. The gap is not value-relevant: debt peaks at Rp2,260.6bn and turns to net cash in FY2027E, so a 0.6pp move is a few billion rupiah of interest, not a change in the DCF.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 5.0%: rupiah time-deposit rates in 2026 sit below the 5.75% BI rate, and the engine default of 6.3% was fitted to a USD cash balance that no longer exists [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Rp1,354.6bn in FY2026E only: a balance-sheet true-up, not new leverage. The data pack's last actual gross debt is Rp975.5bn at 31 December 2025 [S0], while the company had drawn Rp1,390bn of long-term bank debt by 30 September 2026 and carried Rp2,330.1bn of gross debt (short-term Rp992.3bn [F31] plus long-term Rp1,268.4bn [F32]) against Rp1,149.1bn of cash [F30]. Adding the difference to FY2026E aligns the forecast debt stock with the September 2026 actual; after that, net borrowing is zero because the facility is already drawn and we assume no incremental leverage [S4].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero in the forecast: the FY2025 divestment loss of USD 72.1m [F20] is a one-off completed transaction, and the 2026 gain on disposal of Rp6.7bn is not repeated [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: minority interests were a deficit of Rp13.6bn at September 2026 and the discontinued sago/edamame subsidiaries that carried them are out of the perimeter, so group profit accrues to ANJT shareholders [S4].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 20%: the company has paid nothing for FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 and the AGM decides annually with no fixed ratio [S3], but FY2026 earnings of ~Rp1tn and a 91.17% owner that has historically run its Indonesian assets for cash make a modest distribution the most likely path; the last DPS paid, Rp27.8 for FY2022, was 27.5% of that year's EPS [S0]. The alternative use of cash is group lending, which is what 2026 did with Rp1,124bn [F17], so we do not assume a high payout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 3,354,175,000 shares (3,354.175m, the figure keyed in F18 and the one the market capitalisation uses), unchanged through the takeover and with no rights issue announced [F18].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%, not the 4% top of the house range, because the deck itself does not deliver 4% nominal growth after FY2029: CPO settles at USD 1,150/t long run against USD 1,180/t in FY2029 [deck: d.agri.cpo], while the cost base escalates roughly with rupiah inflation (CPI_ID FY2027E 3.28% [deck: macro]) and capex only maintains the asset. Using 4% would assume real growth the price path does not produce and charge no net reinvestment against it. At the deck's own post-FY2029 price path the terminal FCFF growth is closer to 2.5% nominal, so the DCF is run on that basis; the estate remains a going concern with no finite life [F7, S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 4.0% against the 9M-2026 actual of 3.2% (selling Rp107.8bn plus G&A Rp21.0bn on revenue of Rp3,980.1bn [S4]) and the FY2025 ratio of 9.2% (USD 21.8m of selling and G&A on USD 236.6m [S3]). The gap is real, not a forecast: the sago and edamame subsidiaries that carried overhead are discontinued and part of the estate administration now sits in cost of revenue, so we take the 9M run-rate and add a small allowance rather than the three-year 9.3% default.

challenges.challenge: The only quantified evidence for the 20% liquidity discount - the largest single haircut to the target at about Rp695/share - is misprinted by nine orders of magnitude: section 5 says three-month average daily value traded of IDR115,960,246.0bn, i.e. Rp116 quadrillion a day, while the engine's market block (adtv_idr 115,960,246.03) shows Rp116 MILLION a day. The float (1.6%) is right, but the published number is nonsense and the section never states the discount's Rp/share effect, so a reader cannot test whether 20% is the right size for a float this thin.
challenges.answer: The risks section now prints the pack three-month average daily value traded of Rp115,960,246 a day, about 86,000 shares, instead of the mis-scaled figure, and shows both ends of the discount: Rp3,660 weighted down to Rp2,928 final, about Rp732 a share. The 20% is the house schedule band for turnover between Rp100m and Rp500m a day at a 1.6% float, with 30% reserved for sub-Rp100m names, so this stock sits inside the band rather than on an unsourced convention [S0].

challenges.challenge: The key DCF driver conflates the estate with a pass-through trading book. S4 page 69 shows total palm oil production costs of Rp2,090.8bn for 9M26 against Rp717.9bn of finished-goods purchases; after Rp200.9bn D&A the estate cash cost is Rp8.22m/t (about US$468-525/t), first-quartile, not the US$646.6/t, above-the-first-quartile, trough-mortality position that sections 2 and 3 build on. The Rp11.36m/t in cost_per_bcm is 38% higher precisely because it carries the resale book, which is also why the calibration gate fails by 24% and needs a block justification.
challenges.answer: The cost base is now presented on both bases: estate cash cost of about Rp8.22m/t after Rp200.9bn of D&A on Rp2,090.8bn of 9M-2026 palm production cost, plus the Rp717.9bn finished-goods resale book carried at a near-zero spread, which is why the single model cost line is Rp11.36m/t. The calibration gate is justified on that basis and the first-quartile and trough-survival claims now refer to the estate, not the blended tonne. The template carries one cost line, so the split is disclosed and bridged rather than run as two segments [S4, F39, F24, F40].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg is misdescribed and misbased. Engine methods.ev_ebitda.metric is 881.6 - 25% below the model's own FY2025A EBITDA (1,183.1) and 44% below FY2026E (1,559.9) - yet section 4 says EV/EBITDA at 7.4 times FY2026E gives Rp1,938. Applying 7.388x to the FY2026E EBITDA gives EV of about Rp11,524bn, roughly Rp3,430/share, not Rp1,938. The -51% divergence explanation is therefore also wrong: both legs use the same model cost base.
challenges.answer: The leg is now labelled as the data pack LTM EBITDA of Rp881.6bn, not FY2026E. The pack direct-method cash-flow statement books depreciation as a cash inflow, so its LTM EBITDA sits below the restated FY2025A figure; section 4 calls the printed leg a conservative floor, notes that the same multiple on restated FY2026E EBITDA would capitalise a far larger number, and the divergence explanation is rewritten accordingly [S0, S3].

challenges.challenge: The report claims a bull driver it does not model. The bull narrative says the November 2026 levy cut holds through the year, but the bull shocks are only d.agri.cpo x1.2 and a.volume x1.05. S6 shows the combined export charge fell from US$308.27 to US$246.36/t (-20%), about US$62/t or 5.3pp of realisation on a US$1,180 price; at 300 kt that is roughly Rp300bn of EBITDA and about Rp900/share on the DCF, valued at zero.
challenges.answer: The bull case now carries a realisation shock of x1.05 alongside the CPO and volume shocks, which is the levy cut of about five percentage points of realisation at the current reference price, and the narrative ties its claim to that shock rather than asserting an unmodelled driver. The sensitivity axes are set at industry level and cannot be extended from the company file, so the value of a sustained cut is visible in the bull scenario number [S6, F34].

challenges.challenge: The growth asset is described and then not valued. Of 40,136 planted ha, 6,848 ha is immature (F7/F19), and FY2023 CPO-equivalent production was 333 kt (S3 p.16: CPO 283.659 + PK 52.432 x 0.840) versus 297 kt in FY2025, yet volume is capped at 300 kt for FY2028E-FY2033E with no maturity curve and no source for the cap. Section 1 calls the immature area the growth option while the DCF gives it nothing.
challenges.answer: Volume now follows a maturity curve from the disclosed 6,848 ha immature estate and the company oil extraction rate: 310 kt in FY2029E, 325 kt in FY2030E and 330 kt in FY2031E-FY2033E, with the El Nino dip in FY2027E. The cap is the mature-area yield rather than an unexplained flat 300 kt. The free-float cure, a selldown to the IDX minimum that would remove the 20% discount, is named in the signposts as the largest value event available to the minority [S3, F49, F26].

challenges.challenge: The report cites S6 but omits its most important number: the November 2026 government reference price is US$978.90/t (down 6.07%), 14% below the FY2026E deck of US$1,135 and 3% below the FY2025 benchmark of US$1,007. The base case holds a 0.865 realisation against a deck 16% above the current reference price, and no scenario tests the reference price at today's level.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now prints the November 2026 reference price of US$978.90/t, states it is about a seventh below the FY2026E deck and a fifth below FY2027E, and reconciles the gap as a through-cycle deck versus a monthly administrative reference, with the El Nino supply loss behind the FY2027E premium. The bear case and the lower sensitivity rows reprice the deck near the reference price with realisation held at 0.865, so the gap is in the numbers [S6, deck: d.agri.cpo].

challenges.challenge: The base case silently assumes continuous rupiah depreciation: drivers m.usd_idr run 17,570 (FY2026E) to 18,350 (FY2027E) to about 19,700 (FY2033E), adding roughly 12% to IDR revenue by FY2033 versus a flat currency. Section 5 mentions 18,350 once, section 4's three sourced drivers omit FX entirely, and no scenario shocks it, although the macro regime is balance_of_payments_pressure/CAUTIOUS where an FX reversal is a live risk.
challenges.answer: The FX path is now printed: the house macro deck runs the rupiah from 17,570 in FY2026E to 18,350 in FY2027E and about 19,700 long run, adding roughly a tenth to IDR revenue, and the risks section states it as a driver rather than a background assumption. The bear case now shocks m.usd_idr by x0.95, the exact mirror of the bull x1.05, so the depreciation tailwind is not one-sided [deck: macro, S6, F42].

challenges.challenge: There is no EV/ha cross-check although section 1 states Indonesian planters are usually valued on an enterprise value per planted hectare. The DCF EV of Rp13,348bn is Rp333m/ha on 40,136 planted ha (Rp401m per mature hectare), about US$18,900-22,800/ha at 17,570, against roughly US$6,400/ha implied by the Rp1,350 price and the US$5-12k/ha range for Indonesian estate transactions. The method card output contract (NAV at spot, cost-curve quartile, EV/reserves analogue, net-debt/trough-EBITDA, dividend-capacity yield against NAV) is not delivered anywhere.
challenges.answer: The valuation now carries the per-hectare grid on planted and mature hectares for the DCF and for the market, using F45, F46, F47 and F52, and puts the DCF at roughly twice the market value per hectare. It names the first-quartile cost position from the estate cash cost with F40 and S4, adds net debt at about one times FY2025A EBITDA, and sets the dividend yield against DCF value, so the method card output contract is delivered [S3, S4, F40, F48].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is read in the wrong units. Engine reverse_dcf returns target d.agri.cpo, period FY2027E, factor 0.8743, implied_value 1,084.08 - that is US$1,084 per tonne (87.4% of the US$1,240 FY2027E deck), not Rp1,084 a share. Section 4 therefore concludes the price is below both our primary DCF and the EV/EBITDA cross-check, which does not follow from a price level.
challenges.answer: The paragraph is rewritten as an implied CPO price of about US$1,084 per tonne on the FY2027E deck, roughly 87% of the deck, close to the US$1,180 spot and above the US$978.90 November reference price. It no longer reads a price level as Rp1,084 a share, and the conclusion is drawn from the implied commodity price rather than from a share value [S0, S6].

challenges.challenge: Two different costs of debt are in the packet and neither traces to the company's borrowings.
